name: Shasta
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Silver, Shirley Kling. 1966. The Shasta Language. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. viii+243 pp. (eScholarship item 6hj0n3zb; saved PDF is an image scan, 255 pp.)
catalog_locator: Ch. I Phonology, §110 'The syllable', pp. 23-24; §121.2 Pause, pp. 24-25; §130 Tonal accent, p. 25; §161 Vowel length, p. 36; §170.2, p. 40; §181 Vowel and tonal accent distributions, pp. 41-42, with the /ʔe·x/ footnote (marked) at the foot of p. 42; fn. 2 to Chapter I:100, p. 50
catalog_quote: Any syllable containing the sequence /V·/ is heavy; all others are light. A heavy syllable is strongly stressed; a light syllable is weakly stressed. While it is possible for one heavy syllable to have less stress than another, and for one light syllable to have more stress than another light syllable, it is always the case that a heavy syllable is more strongly stressed than a light one. In disyllabic sequences, either light-light or heavy-heavy, both syllables are equally stressed. In a sequence of three or more light syllables, or three or more heavy syllables, the penultimate syllable receives the most stress. In polysyllabic sequences of light and heavy syllables, if the penultimate syllable is light, the first preceding heavy syllable will be the most strongly stressed. [p. 24] An open syllable is one ending in V [·][L] (where L = /y/, /w/); any other syllable is closed. A light open syllable occurring between two heavy syllables is unstressed.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable from syllable weight, where heavy = long vowel (/V·/). Heavy syllables are strongly stressed and light ones weakly; among syllables of equal weight (three or more all-light or all-heavy) the penultimate is most prominent; in mixed words with a light penult the nearest heavy syllable to its left carries the main stress; disyllables of equal weight have level stress; a light open syllable sandwiched between heavies is unstressed. Independently of stress, every syllable bears one of two contrastive level pitches (high vs low), which Silver calls the tonal accent; high pitch is marked with an acute in her transcription.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; Silver speaks of degrees of 'heavy and light stress' across the utterance (all heavy syllables strongly stressed, light ones weakly) rather than a single secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: A light open syllable between two heavy syllables is unstressed (p. 24). Prepausal degrees of heavy/light stress vary through the utterance and condition the height of the tonal accent (p. 24-25); vowel length may drop before pause while its strong stress remains (p. 25). One anomalous falling tonal accent in the loan /tíi/ 'tea' (§170.2, p. 40); the interjection /ʔe·x/ has low pitch with extra length and extra heavy stress (fn., p. 42).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'utterance' bounded by pause, which Silver equates with the syntactically defined word (p. 25: pause 'corresponds.. to the boundaries of the word as it is defined by the syntactic rules'; the speaker's own 'word' matched it). Stress is described as non-distinctive prominence riding on syllable weight; prepausal variation in stress, pitch and length is 'not.. systematically distinctive' (p. 25). Alongside this, §130 (p. 25) states a contrastive pitch system: 'The Shasta tonal system consists of two contrastive level pitches, high (/´/) and low (unmarked). Every syllable occurs with either high or low pitch'; footnote 2 (p. 50): all but two monosyllables in the corpus carry high pitch. Silver (p. 36, §161) also says precise statements on the interaction of syllable sequences, vowel length and stress could not be formulated. Data: Sargent Sambo (main informant) and Clara Wicks, 1957 onward.
new_statements.identity_note: Silver 1966 describes the Shasta of Sargent Sambo (Oregon/Shasta Valley Shasta ancestry, with kammatwa maternal grandmother) and Clara Wicks, recorded 1957 onward; this is Shasta proper, glottocode shas1239, not the other Shastan languages (Konomihu kono1241, New River Shasta newr1237, Okwanuchu okwa1235), which are only touched in the introduction and bibliography.
